text: With what speed should a galaxy move outward with respect to earth so that the sodium-D line at wavelength 5890 $A^{o}$ is observed at 5896 $A^{o}$ ?
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 20th July Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$f=f_{0}\sqrt{\frac{1+β}{1-β}}$

$β=\frac{v}{c}$

$\frac{f}{f_{0}}=\sqrt{\frac{1+β}{1-β}}$

$\left (1+\frac{\Delta f}{f_{0}}\right )^{2}=(1+β)(1-β)^{-1}$

$β$ is small compared to 1

$\left (1+\frac{2\Delta f}{f_{0}}\right )=(1+2β)$

$β=\frac{\Delta f}{f_{0}}=\frac{v}{c}$

$v=6\times \frac{c}{5890}=305.6$ km/s

text:
Consider a binary star system of star A and star B with masses $m_{A}$ and $m_{B}$ revolving in a circular orbit of radii $r_{A}$ an $r_{B}$, respectively. If $T_{A}$ and $T_{B}$ are the time period of star A and star B, respectively,

Then :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 20th July Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In a binary star system, the two stars orbit around a common center of mass. When considering periods of revolution, Kepler's Third Law comes into play. This law states that the square of the period of revolution (T) is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis (r) of the orbit. It's often written in the following form for a single object orbiting another:

T² ∝ r³

For a binary star system, this would still hold true. The periods of revolution for both stars A and B will be the same because they are both orbiting the same common center of mass, regardless of their individual masses or individual orbital radii. In other words, star A and star B complete one orbit in the same amount of time.

So, Option B: $T_{A} = T_{B}$ is correct.

The other options (Option A, C, and D) would not be correct. Kepler's Third Law is not a ratio between the periods and radii of two different bodies, and the periods do not depend on the masses of the individual stars or their individual distances from the center of mass.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2021 (Online) 20th July Evening Shift

text: Two small drops of mercury each of radius R coalesce to form a single large drop. The ratio of total surface energy before and after the change is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 20th July Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The volume of a sphere is given by $\frac{4}{3}πR^{3}$.

So the volume of the two small mercury drops each of radius $R$ is $2\times \frac{4}{3}πR^{3}$.

When they coalesce to form a larger drop, the volume is conserved. So, the volume of the larger drop is also $2\times \frac{4}{3}πR^{3}$.

Let's denote the radius of this large drop as $R^{'}$.

Therefore, $2\times \frac{4}{3}πR^{3}=\frac{4}{3}πR^{'}^{3}$.

Solving for $R^{'}$, we get $R^{'}=2^{1/3}R$.

Now, the surface energy of a sphere is proportional to its surface area, and the surface area of a sphere is given by $4πR^{2}$.

So, the ratio of total surface energy before and after the change is:

$\frac{2\times 4πR^{2}}{4π(2^{1/3}R)^{2}}=\frac{2}{2^{2/3}}=2^{1/3}:1$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2021 (Online) 20th July Evening Shift

solution.body:
I in both cases is about point of contact 

Ring

text:
For the forward biased diode characteristics shown in the figure, the dynamic resistance at $I_{D} = 3 mA$ will be $__________$ $\Omega$.


[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 20th July Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
From the graph, the characteristic is nearly a straight line between $(0.65\text{V},1\text{mA})$ and $(0.75\text{V},5\text{mA})$, and $I_{D}=3\text{mA}$ (at $0.70\text{V}$) lies on this segment.

The dynamic resistance is the inverse slope of the characteristic there:

$r_{d}=\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}=\dfrac{0.75-0.65}{(5-1)\times 10^{-3}}=\dfrac{0.10}{4\times 10^{-3}}=25\Omega$

Hence, the answer is 25.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2021 (Online) 20th July Evening Shift
